title: Nepal Flood Death Toll Surges Past 330 as Glacier Collapse Scale Becomes Clear
excerpt: Scientists confirm an ice-rock avalanche, not an earthquake, triggered one of Nepal's worst natural disasters, with over 900 people still missing including dozens of Americans and 177 Indian pilgrims.
body:
• Death toll from the Nepal-Tibet border floods has surged to 332, with over 900 people still missing including 177 Indian pilgrims, 63 Americans, and nationals from more than 20 countries
  • Scientists confirm a massive glacier collapse — not an earthquake — sent an ice-rock avalanche down the Lhende Khola river, triggering catastrophic flash floods that tore through the Trishuli river system
  • UNICEF has mobilized emergency teams and supplies, dispatching hygiene kits, medical tents, and therapeutic food for children, while working to reunite separated families
  • Nine hydroelectric facilities, 35 motorable bridges, 45 suspension bridges, and 40 km of paved roads were destroyed across eight districts

The death toll from Wednesday's catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border has more than doubled in 24 hours, with Nepali police confirming at least 332 people dead across eight districts as of Thursday afternoon. More than 900 people remain missing, many of them foreign tourists and pilgrims, in what scientists are calling one of the largest glacial disaster events in Himalayan history.

What Caused the Disaster

At 8:40 a.m. local time on Wednesday, August 26, the lower portion of a Himalayan glacier collapsed and crashed onto the valley floor roughly 20 km northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing between Nepal and China's Tibet. Initial reports pointed to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, but the U.S. Geological Survey later clarified that the seismic event was generated by the collapse itself — the force of glacial rock and ice slamming into the earth, followed by massive debris flow.

https://x.com/coolnotesix/status/2092984982801457297

The avalanche of ice, rock, and mud swept down the Lhende Khola river, which runs along the mountainous Nepal-Tibet border. It slammed into Gyirong port on the Tibetan side and then tore through Nepal's Trishuli river system, destroying villages, roads, and hydropower infrastructure across more than 60 miles.

"The force of this thing is just almost incomprehensible. It's one of the largest events of its kind that I've seen in some 30 years of research."

— Alton Byers, Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado Boulder

Before-and-after satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters showed lush green mountainside now buried under brown sediment. Earth scientist Dan Shugar of the University of Calgary noted that glaciers in the valley had been covered in snow the day before and were reduced to bare ice after the collapse, suggesting unusually warm conditions preceded the event.

Hundreds of Foreigners Missing

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) in Kathmandu confirmed the disaster originated from a high-altitude ice-rock avalanche on the Tibetan side. Among the nearly 1,500 people unaccounted for across both countries are an estimated 750 foreigners.

In Nepal alone, the missing include 177 Indians — many on a pilgrimage to the sacred Kailash Mansarovar site — 63 Americans, 53 Ukrainians, 34 Australians, 33 British nationals, 28 Malaysians, and 25 Canadians, according to Reuters. Nine South Korean workers at a hydropower plant are also unaccounted for. Citizens from more than 20 additional countries have been reported missing.

On the Chinese side, state broadcaster CCTV reported at least three deaths in Tibet with 558 people missing, though authorities have not clarified whether those figures overlap with Nepal's count. A large barrier lake has formed where two rivers converge in Nepal, and Chinese authorities have warned it could trigger further flooding.

Rescue Operations and International Response

Nepal has mobilized more than 5,000 army and police personnel for search and rescue. Helicopters are ferrying tents, food, and emergency supplies — much of it provided by India, which is coordinating closely with Kathmandu. By Thursday, 125 people had been rescued including 20 foreigners, according to Nepal Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet. However, downed power lines, destroyed bridges, and deep flood sediment are severely hampering ground access.

UNICEF has deployed emergency teams to the hardest-hit communities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. Pre-positioned supplies including medical tents, hygiene kits, bed nets, newborn kits, and ready-to-use therapeutic food for malnourished children are being dispatched. Mental health teams have been mobilized, and UNICEF is working to identify and reunite children separated from their families.

The United Nations is mobilizing additional supplies and personnel. South Korea is sending a rapid-response team, and India has issued flood alerts downstream — about 5,000 people were evacuated in Bihar as a precaution.

Climate Change and the Himalayan Risk

Nepal's snow-capped mountains lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global warming, according to a 2023 UN assessment. While scientists cautioned it is too early to definitively link this specific event to climate change, the pattern is unmistakable.

"Flood events of various origins are being seen with increasing frequency and magnitude" as high-mountain regions warm faster than most of the planet, said Byers. A similar disaster struck Uttarakhand, India, in February 2021, when 30 million cubic meters of rock and ice swept down a mountain, killing over 200 people and destroying two hydropower plants. The infrastructure damage in Nepal mirrors that event: nine hydroelectric facilities, 35 motorable bridges, 45 suspension bridges, and 40 km of paved roads have been destroyed.

What to Watch

Rescue operations remain the immediate priority, but authorities are also monitoring the barrier lake for signs of further flooding. With infrastructure devastated and communications cut in many areas, the full scope of casualties may not be known for days. India's External Affairs Ministry has set up emergency helplines, and the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu is assisting in efforts to locate the 177 missing Indian nationals.
